hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, the numeric age of the late Chalk (Late Cretaceous, the 'latter part of the Secondary period') in the International Chronostratigraphic Chart is about 300 million years or more before present.
pass_criterion: The ICS chart gives the top of the Cretaceous (Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition) an age of at least 225 Ma (within 25% of 300 Ma, or older). The same threshold applies to the Campanian–Maastrichtian ages, which are the youngest Chalk stages.
fail_criterion: The ICS chart gives the top of the Cretaceous and the Campanian–Maastrichtian stages ages below 225 Ma. This would show that 'roughly 300 million years since the late Chalk' (or more) is off by more than 25%. A value near 66 Ma would fall in this range.
interpretation: 'Latter part of the Secondary period' is read as the Late Cretaceous. 'Since the late Chalk' is read as the time from the youngest Chalk Group strata (Campanian–Maastrichtian) to the present. Darwin's 'Secondary' corresponds to the Mesozoic. The numeric ages come from the ICS chart's boundary ages in Ma. The test compares this age with Darwin's 306,662,400 years. It does not test the erosion rate itself. The claim is a duration inferred from the rate, so the test checks that duration against the radiometrically calibrated timescale.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: The chart lists numeric boundary ages in Ma for each stage and system. The fields used are the base age of the Paleogene (the top of the Cretaceous) and the base and top ages of the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages. These give the elapsed time since the late Chalk, which is compared directly with Darwin's ~300 Myr.
